message.content:
Below is a concise, practical guide to the key rights you have as a residential tenant in Texas.  (This is not legal advice; if you have a specific dispute, consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.)

| # | Right | What it means | Typical Texas law / statute |
|---|-------|---------------|-----------------------------|
| **1** | **Right to a habitable dwelling** | Your landlord must keep the property in a safe, livable condition—plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc. | Texas Property Code § 92.001‑92.003 |
| **2** | **Right to privacy** | Landlord may enter only with reasonable notice (usually 24 hrs) and for legitimate reasons (repairs, inspections, showing to prospective tenants). | § 92.006 |
| **3** | **Right to a written lease (if you sign one)** | A lease should spell out rent amount, due date, security deposit limits, lease term, and any rules. | § 92.001 |
| **4** | **Right to a security deposit limit** | Landlord can hold up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit or **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit. | § 92.008 |
| **5** | **Right to a security‑deposit return** | Landlord must return the deposit (minus lawful deductions) within **30 days** after you move out, unless you agree otherwise in writing. | § 92.008 |
| **6** | **Right to receive a written itemized list of deductions** | If the landlord keeps any part of the deposit, they must provide a written statement of damages and costs. | § 92.008 |
| **7** | **Right to a fair eviction process** | Landlord must give proper notice (30 days for month‑to‑month, 60 days for longer leases) and file a court action if you don’t comply. | § 92.006 |
| **8** | **Right to challenge unlawful eviction** | You can file a **“unlawful detainer”** defense if the landlord violated notice requirements or used illegal tactics. | § 92.006 |
| **9** | **Right to a written notice of rent increase** | For month‑to‑month tenants, a 30‑day notice is required for a rent increase. | § 92.006 |
| **10** | **Right to a written lease amendment** | Any changes to the lease must be in writing and signed by both parties. | § 92.001 |
| **11** | **Right to a safe environment** | Landlord must address health hazards (lead paint, mold, radon, etc.) promptly. | § 92.001 |
| **12** | **Right to a copy of the lease** | Landlord must provide you with a copy of the lease or lease agreement. | § 92.001 |
| **13** | **Right to a “no‑trespassing” notice** | Landlord cannot lock you out or deny access without following legal eviction procedures. | § 92.006 |
| **14** | **Right to a “reasonable” notice for repairs** | Landlord must give notice before entering for repairs, except in emergencies. | § 92.006 |
| **15** | **Right to a “reasonable” notice for rent increases** | Landlord must give at least 30 days’ notice for a rent increase. | § 92.006 |
| **16** | **Right to a “reasonable” notice for lease termination** | Landlord must give at least 30 days’ notice to terminate a month‑to‑month lease. | § 92.006 |
| **17** | **Right to a “reasonable” notice for lease renewal** | Landlord must give notice if they intend not to renew. | § 92.006 |
| **18** | **Right to a “reasonable” notice for lease termination by tenant** | You can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ notice. | § 92.006 |
| **19** | **Right to a “reasonable” notice for lease termination by landlord** | Landlord must give at least 30 days’ notice to terminate a month‑to‑month lease. | § 92.006 |
| **20** | **Right to a “reasonable” notice for lease termination by landlord** | Landlord must give at least 30 days’ notice to terminate a month‑to‑month lease. | § 92.006 |

---

### How to Exercise These Rights

1. **Keep Records**  
   - Save copies of the lease, rent receipts, emails, texts, and any written communication with your landlord.  
   - Take photos or videos of any maintenance issues.

2. **Use Written Notices**  
   - Send any complaints or requests in writing (email or certified mail) so you have proof of delivery.

3. **Know the Notice Periods**  
   - For month‑to‑month: 30‑day notice to terminate or increase rent.  
   - For longer leases: 60‑day notice to terminate or increase rent.

4. **File a Complaint**  
   - If your landlord violates your rights, you can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs, or your local housing agency.

5. **Seek Mediation**  
   - Many cities offer free or low‑cost mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes.

6. **Legal Action**  
   - If the landlord fails to comply, you can file a lawsuit in the appropriate county court (unlawful detainer action).  
   - Small claims court can handle disputes up to $20,000.

---

### Useful Resources

| Resource | What it Offers | Link |
|----------|----------------|------|
| **Texas Attorney General – Tenant Rights** | Guides, FAQs, and complaint forms | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/ |
| **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs** | Information on fair housing, landlord‑tenant laws | https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us/ |
| **Texas Legal Services Center** | Free legal help for low‑income residents | https://www.texaslegalservices.org/ |
| **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Advocacy, workshops, and legal clinics | Search “tenant rights organization Texas” |
| **Texas Property Code** | Full statutory text | https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/ |

---

### Quick Checklist Before Moving In

- [ ] Get a **written lease** (or lease agreement).  
- [ ] Verify the **security deposit** amount (max 1–2 months’ rent).  
- [ ] Inspect the unit and document any existing damage.  
- [ ] Confirm the landlord’s contact info and emergency procedures.  
- [ ] Keep a copy of the lease and any correspondence.

---

#### Bottom Line

As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, privacy, a clear lease, a limited security deposit, and a fair eviction process.  If your landlord violates any of these rights, you can document the issue, send written notices, file complaints, and ultimately pursue legal action if necessary.  For personalized guidance, consider contacting a local tenant‑rights group or an attorney.
